Why We Built Design Creativity Bench: Measuring What AI Coding Benchmarks Miss

Community Article Published
November 2, 2026 Upvote 4 Mukund Mohan babushkaboy Kombai Sourabh Upreti sourabhsss Kombai
Today’s AI models can build functional, feature-rich interfaces. Their technical capabilities have advanced rapidly and are measured across a growing number of benchmarks. Their ability to make creative design decisions remains a more open question.
At Kombai, we build AI tools for frontend and design engineering. We often see polished interfaces that repeat familiar layouts across different products. Several models given the same brief can arrive at similar designs; a single model given different product contexts may change little beyond labels and colors.
We built Design Creativity Bench (DCB) to investigate this pattern. When a brief leaves room for many valid solutions, how creatively do models use that freedom?

What existing evaluations tell us

SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench evaluate engineering task completion. VIBE Bench asks whether generated applications build, run, work under interaction, and present well. Design Arena collects human preferences between design outputs.
These evaluations cover capabilities users need. But an interface can satisfy its requirements and win a preference comparison while resembling the designs models produce for many other products.
Anti-“slop” checklists address part of the problem by flagging familiar colors, typography, or card layouts. Repetition also appears in information architecture and composition, and avoiding one recognizable style can push models toward another. We wanted a measurement grounded in the generated designs themselves.

Giving models room to be creative

The study evaluated 15 frontier models across 80 UI tasks, each adapted to two product domains. That produced 160 briefs and 2,400 standalone HTML interfaces, alongside human reference designs created for the same briefs.
Each pair shares a goal and a screen type(dashboard, pricing page etc). The briefs specify what the interface must contain and accomplish, while leaving layout, hierarchy, and visual style open.
Consider a dispatcher screen for a residential appliance-repair company and one for a commercial HVAC contractor. Both involve scheduling technicians. But the HVAC dispatcher may need to coordinate crewed jobs, restricted site-access windows, and recurring maintenance. Those requirements give a designer reasons to reconsider how the work is organized and which information deserves prominence.
We evaluate the resulting designs across three dimensions:

Originality: How distinct a model’s designs are from those of other models for the same brief. Comparisons exclude models from the same lab, so the score is relative to the evaluated panel.
Creative range: How much a model’s designs vary across the two product contexts in a task pair.
Appropriateness: The share of the brief’s acceptance criteria that a design satisfies, including required content, controls, and correct values.
Appropriateness keeps requirement satisfaction in view alongside creative diversity. A design that looks different because it omits required information has not successfully fulfilled the brief.

Measuring distinctiveness

We render each HTML interface in a browser, divide the page into structural segments, and compare them using Embedding and learned projections. These projections are trained to reduce sensitivity to changes such as copy, spacing, and theme while responding more strongly to structural edits.
The similarity calculation weights information architecture at 90% and the color system at 10%. We then calculate distinctiveness as “one minus similarity”: higher values indicate less similar designs.
We validated the scorer against human judgments and controlled design changes. On one set of pairwise comparisons, it agreed with the pooled human choice 82.5% of the time. On a separate judgment set that was not used to select or tune the scorer, it achieved an AUC of 0.85. The paper describes the method and validation in detail.

What the study found

Models converge on similar designs. Average distinctiveness between models working from the same brief was 0.592, compared with 0.764 between human and model designs. Model outputs resembled one another more than they resembled the human reference. This human-model comparison does not measure differences between human designers.
Models show less creative range across contexts. Average creative range was 0.581 across the models, compared with 0.902 for the human reference. Even with the product domain and content changed, models retained more of the same design approach across paired briefs.
Requirement satisfaction remains high. Every model in the original panel met more than 90% of the evaluated acceptance criteria. Claude Opus 5.5 reached 99.2%, compared with 98.0% for the human reference. The models could generally build the requested screens while exploring a narrower range of designs.
Originality and creative range can diverge. GPT-6 Astra had the highest originality in the paper’s panel, at 0.646, yet its creative range was 0.472, among the narrowest. It stood apart from its peers while repeating its own approach across product contexts. Across the core panel, we found no statistically significant rank association between the two measures.
These results explain why we report the dimensions separately. A model’s distinctive style can coexist with limited creative range, and strong requirement satisfaction can coexist with both.
The live leaderboard includes additional evaluations. The findings above refer to the paper’s original 15-model study.

How to interpret the results

DCB measures creativity through variation among designs and their ability to satisfy a brief. Distinctiveness alone does not establish aesthetic quality or show that every change suits the product. Appropriateness is also limited to the evaluated criteria; it is not a comprehensive assessment of accessibility, usability, or production readiness.
The study covers desktop interfaces, a finite set of tasks, and a learned similarity metric. Each model generated its designs in fresh contexts, using default API sampling and no specialized diversity-seeking prompts. The results describe behavior under those conditions, rather than the full range a model might achieve with different prompting or iteration.
The human reference also needs context. Multiple designers created it using public inspiration libraries. It supports comparisons with human-designed solutions to the same briefs, but does not measure one designer’s creative range or establish that every human designer is more creative than every model.
We have not identified why models converge. Training data, training objectives, post-training, and inference settings remain possible areas for investigation.

Building on the research

For model and tool builders, DCB offers a way to test whether prompting, sampling, or design-directed workflows increase creative range while preserving appropriateness. For evaluation researchers, it makes an aspect of creativity measurable that is difficult to infer from engineering scores or preference rankings.
The public dataset contains 300 HTML designs across 20 prompts, representing 10 paired tasks evaluated across 15 models. It includes acceptance criteria, model configurations, generation instructions, published scores, and controlled design-change studies. We have also released precomputed features and embeddings and projection training data.
This release is a reproducibility subset. Scores calculated on its public prompts should not be compared directly with the paper’s full evaluation.
We welcome work extending the benchmark to more product contexts and interface types, as well as further human evaluation of the scorer. Read the paper, inspect the prompts and generated designs, and test where the measurement holds up or needs to improve.
